item.title: DOJ wants Pete Hegseth's anti-trans slurs excluded from discrimination trial
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is standing by his descriptions of transgender people as “weird” and his use of an anti-trans slur. The Trump administration, meanwhile, is asking a federal judge to prevent those statements from being used as evidence that its ban on transgender people’s military service is discriminatory. The administration’s effort to keep Hegseth’s own words out of evidence is detailed in a series of court filings submitted Friday in Talbott v. Trump , a lawsuit brought by transgender troops fighting to remain in uniform. The plaintiffs are represented by a coalition of leading LGBTQ+ civil rights organizations and prominent litigation firms, including GLAD Law , the National Center for LGBTQ Rights , Wardenski P.C. , Zalkind Duncan & Bernstein LLP , Kropf Moseley Schmitt PLLC and international law firm O’Melveny & Myers LLP . In sworn written answers , Hegseth defended his language, reiterated his support for excluding trans troops and said he disagreed with nothing in President Donald Trump’s executive order restricting their service. The Justice Department is also trying to exclude testimony from former Pentagon officials who dispute the administration’s military readiness claims. In another filing, government lawyers admit that the policy cuts short some military careers. A hearing scheduled for Monday before Washington, D.C. , U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes . Related: ‘This is where we are’: Federal Judge Ana Reyes reports death threats to her family amid Trump attacks Hegseth stands by his words Hegseth’s answers, signed October 28 under penalty of perjury, offer an account of how he views the people his department is trying to remove from military service. Attorneys asked him about a passage from his 2024 book, The War on Warriors , in which he described transgender people as pretending to be members of another sex and called that “weird.” “Men pretending to be women is ‘weird’ because men cannot be women and women cannot be men,” Hegseth wrote in the court filing. Another question addressed his previous references to transgender people as “dudes in dresses” and using an anti-transgender slur. Hegseth repeated both expressions, saying people covered by the Pentagon’s restrictions on gender dysphoria should be excluded. Asked which statements in Trump’s executive order he personally disagreed with, Hegseth answered, “None.” He also defended his May 2025 declaration, “No More Trans @ DoD,” posted after the U.S. Supreme Court allowed the administration to enforce the ban while litigation continued. “I, like many others, occasionally use the term ‘trans’ as shorthand for individuals with gender dysphoria,” Hegseth wrote. Gender dysphoria refers to clinically significant distress that can arise when a person’s gender identity differs from their sex assigned at birth. Not all transgender people experience gender dysphoria, and being transgender is not a mental illness. Gender-affirming care is the treatment for that distress. The government argues that its policy targets a medical diagnosis rather than transgender identity. The plaintiffs contend that the medical language is being used to remove transgender people regardless of their qualifications. Related: Pete Hegseth may have to testify under oath about his anti-trans slurs. A federal judge put the DOJ on notice The judge already demanded answers The written responses follow an October 14 hearing that The Advocate previously covered, when Reyes challenged government attorneys over efforts to shield Hegseth from questioning about his remarks. “The government got up here and told me that when he tweeted transgender people are excluded from the military, he did not mean transgender people are excluded from the military,” Reyes said. Plaintiffs sought a seven-hour deposition, which would have required Hegseth to answer attorneys’ questions under oath. Reyes declined to order that extensive questioning, instead requiring him to answer 10 written questions. But she warned that inadequate responses could lead to a limited, one-hour deposition. “I am very aware that he is the secretary of defense and has a lot of constraints on his time, but he has time to tweet, and he has time to put out videos, and he has time to speak to the generals,” Reyes said. She also offered to supervise any deposition herself. “If they give questions and the responses are a bunch of non-answers, totally fine, but then we’re going to get back into deposition world,” she warned. Related: Trump administration tells federal judge to ignore Pete Hegseth’s anti-trans posts The government says the slurs don’t prove discrimination The Justice Department does not dispute that Hegseth made the statements. Instead, it argues that they should not be used to establish discriminatory intent. Its motion specifically identifies his references to “trans lunacy,” “dudes in dresses” and the anti-transgender slur, arguing that they reflect concerns about medical fitness, military discipline and deployability rather than unconstitutional hostility. A separate filing asks Reyes to determine whom the policy targets by examining its written rules rather than statements made by officials promoting it. In March 2025, Reyes temporarily blocked the ban , calling it “soaked in animus and dripping with pretext,” and finding that the policy was likely driven by discrimination and supported by explanations that concealed its purpose. Former Pentagon officials challenge the readiness claims The administration is also trying to exclude testimony from former Pentagon leaders who oversaw military personnel policies when transgender troops served openly. Shawn Skelly, a retired Navy commander and former senior readiness official, says no readiness or unit cohesion problems attributable to transgender service reached her office. Former Army personnel official Yvette Bourcicot argues that the administration’s waiver requirements are effectively impossible for many troops who transitioned under previously approved military policies. Ashish Vazirani, a former acting undersecretary of defense, wrote in a report that transition-related healthcare averaged $5.2 million annually over 10 fiscal years, less than 0.01 percent of the military health system’s approximately $60.2 billion fiscal 2024 budget. Former Air Force personnel official Alex Wagner argues that the policy allows qualified troops to be discharged without individual evidence that their medical circumstances interfere with their duties. The Justice Department disputes whether the former officials can reliably assess the current policy and argues that courts should defer to current military leadership. The administration acknowledges careers are being cut short In a motion seeking to exclude testimony from retired Army Maj. Gen. James Young, the Justice Department agreed that the ban ends some military careers prematurely. “Defendants acknowledge as a factual matter that absent a waiver, some service members who fall within the policy do in fact have their careers curtailed,” government lawyers wrote. Young argues that forced separation can cost troops future earnings, retirement benefits and veterans’ compensation. The government disputes his financial projections but acknowledges the underlying career disruption. The administration also withdrew its notice that it intended to seek summary judgment Friday, abandoning its previously announced effort to have the case decided without trial. Monday’s scheduled hearing has been moved online. In a Saturday order, Reyes directed the parties to appear by teleconference at 4 p.m. Eastern after they requested the proceeding to address a dispute over evidence gathering. A two-week bench trial is scheduled to begin on January 4. This article originally appeared on Advocate: Pete Hegseth defended his anti-trans slurs under penalty of perjury. The DOJ wants them excluded from trial RELATED ‘This is where we are’: Federal Judge Ana Reyes reports death threats to her family amid Trump attacks Pete Hegseth may have to testify under oath about his anti-trans slurs. A federal judge put the DOJ on notice Trump administration tells federal judge to ignore Pete Hegseth’s anti-trans posts This article originally appeared on The Advocate at https://www.advocate.com/politics/national/doj-moves-strike-hegseth-words

item.title: Van Hollen says Schumer's team is trying to 'instill fear' to retain Senate leadership
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen touted his chances of becoming Senate majority leader when Democrats take control of the Senate in January, accusing current leader Sen. Chuck Schumer of trying to scare Democrats into supporting his continued leadership. "I think there's a very open lane here. The Schumer team's put out a lot of misinformation," Van Hollen told ABC News' "This Week" co-anchor Martha Raddatz in an interview on Sunday. "They're essentially trying to instill fear in people who may say that they're going to support me as a new leader ... We just had a great day for our democracy around the country. How about a little democracy in the Senate Democratic Caucus?" In a post on social media this week, Schumer wrote that he welcomes "any discussion about the future of our caucus," continuing to say that he has "the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader." ABC News - PHOTO: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) appears on ABC's "This Week." Schumer's optimism came as several Democratic senators and others elected in this month's midterm elections expressed the desire for new leadership in Washington, despite Schumer's efforts in recruiting candidates who led the party to overwhelming control of the Senate. Van Hollen, who announced his candidacy to challenge Schumer on Thursday night, said voters made clear on election day that they oppose President Donald Trump, but clarified their votes weren't a ringing endorsement of his party either. Van Hollen told Raddatz he believes this leadership vote is a chance to regain their trust. "They rejected Trump's policy, his wars, his corruption, the high cost. But they haven't fully hired the Democrats. We have a chance, but we need to earn the people's trust. And I don't think you earn people's trust by simply going back to business as usual and status quo," Van Hollen said. Schumer and Van Hollen are facing off for Senate majority leader. What do Democrats think? Van Hollen also responded to the resignation of Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang amid his admitting to an affair reported to be with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang. Van Hollen told Raddatz he's "very concerned" about the national security implications of the unfolding scandal. "He has gotten the president to allow Nvidia to send very high-end chips to China against the advice of folks in the national security arena," Van Hollen said, suggesting that Alice Huang may have been part of an effort to divert such chips to China. Alice Huang was a top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company with access to Nvidia's most powerful chips, which under U.S. law cannot be imported into China. The New York Times reported that Megaspeed has been under investigation by the U.S. since 2024 for potentially smuggling those chips into China, allegations Beijing has denied. Huang, who admitted to having an affair last Sunday, resigned from the company he's led since founding it in 1993. His decision to step down came after reports of an additional affair with an Nvidia employee, adding to the growing controversy spawned by reports of his relationship with Alice Huang and her alleged role as a Chinese intelligence asset. 1-on-1 with Sen. Chris Van Hollen Van Hollen, who sits on both the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and Senate Banking Committee, rebutted Trump's claims that he was not briefed about the relationship ahead of his trip to China in May of this year, which Jensen Huang accompanied the president on. "This is a president who lies to the American public all the time, and this is why we need an investigation. We need people testifying," Van Hollen told Raddatz. "I do believe he was briefed. I think all the information that I've seen suggests that this would not have escaped the attention of the president of the United States." This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Politics/van-hollen-schumer-instill-fear-retain-senate-leadership/story?id=138155548

item.title: Transportation secretary says he doesn't apologize for FAA's nationwide ground stop
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Sunday declined to apologize for the nationwide ground stop on Friday that stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country following a router issue that derailed air traffic control communications. Instead, the secretary blamed his predecessors and previous presidential administrations that he said did not do enough to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system. “It happened on my watch, but we have to be clear: I am moving at an incredible speed that no one has done at the FAA or in decades, and I’m proud of the work we’re doing, the attention we’re bringing to this issue,” Duffy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press.” “But I can’t apologize for what was passed off to us, and I can’t blame Republicans or Democrats because it’s all of them.” The secretary also blamed “30 years of a lack of investment,” from the country’s previous leaders. “Why they didn’t do that I don’t know, but they gave me a system that needs to be fixed, and President [Donald] Trump and I are going to fix it,” he added. His remarks come less than two days after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop that lasted several hours, leading to thousands of flight cancellations beginning on Friday and continuing through the weekend. A stranded traveler sleeps Saturday in the terminal in Orlando, Fla. ( Christopher Beckett / NurPhoto via Getty) FAA contractor L3Harris was working on replacing a copper line with a fiber line at a remote site when the work led a router to overwhelm the national FAA telecommunications network, Duffy said Saturday. Duffy also said Sunday on “Meet the Press” that he expects airports and airlines to resume normal operations by the end of the day or early Monday morning. “By the end of today, into tomorrow, I think we’ll be back to normal,” he said, adding that Friday’s ground stop led airplanes and flight crews to be “out of position.” “It takes some time for the airlines to rechoreograph all of their crews and aircraft. We’re going to start seeing things get better today, but I think back to normal tomorrow,” Duffy said. The secretary also demurred when asked whether he could guarantee that a similar travel disruption won’t happen in the future. “First we have to figure out what happened. Was this a faulty installation by L3Harris that was doing their work for us? Was it a fault of the router itself? We have to do that investigation and make sure we take precautions. We don’t want to shut down the airspace,” Duffy told “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker. “We’re going to figure out what was the root cause and then move forward from there, fixing how we do business at the FAA,” he added. Duffy also reiterated a call he’s made all weekend for more funding from Congress to modernize the nationwide air traffic control system, which has long been outdated and faced problems. “The president, since he came to office, has been pushing for modernization of the airspace. Before I was even sworn in, he brought this up,” the secretary said, pointing to $12.5 billion that was allocated for air traffic control improvements in a GOP-backed spending bill last year. “The Congress was very specific in how I spend that money. I have a certain allotment for radar, a certain allotment for radios, a certain allotment for building new infrastructure for my centers for air traffic controllers. They didn’t give me money for telecom. They didn’t give me money for new software,” Duffy said. “I’m coming back to Congress and the American people to explain all the great work we’re doing right now,” he continued. “We’re going to spend that $12.5 billion by the end of 2028, but I need the rest of the money for software and a new telecom architecture that will be way more resilient. I need that money so I can start that build.” On Saturday, NBC News reported that on Thursday, just one day before the ground stop, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought sent a letter to members of Congress asking lawmakers for $30.1 billion to upgrade the United States’ aging airports and air traffic control system. They wrote: “This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace — delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure. These investments will address current challenges, including weather-related delays, while preparing the National Airspace System for emerging demands, such as safely integrating air traffic with the growing space industry.” On Sunday, Duffy urged Congress to “just do it.” “I’m doing all I can to keep people safe,” he said. “But I’m also telling you, if you don’t give us the resources, we can’t complete the job. And this is — of all the partisanship — this is the most bipartisan thing in all of Washington. Democrats, Republicans, the president, everyone agrees on this. Let’s just do it.” In a statement Sunday in response to questions about how the president plans to urge Congress to appropriate funds for the air traffic control infrastructure, White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said, “The Trump administration immediately stepped into action at the first sign of issue to ensure the safety and security of all Americans. President Trump put the right leadership into place to effectively handle moments like these, and yesterday, all relevant leaders came together to coordinate a plan that put the safety of the American people first.” She added, “This administration will continue to monitor this situation and communicate to the American people through every necessary means.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/trump-administration/transportation-secretary-apologize-nationwide-ground-stop-airports-rcna609397

item.title: Auction of $180 million Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Vincent van Gogh's Châtaigniers en fleurs is displayed ahead of this week's auction [Reuters] Auction house Sotheby's says it is working to resolve a dispute over the intended sale of a painting by Vincent van Gogh. Châtaigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom"), which carries an estimated value of $180m (£136m), is due to go under the hammer in New York on Wednesday. But representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - say it may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis. Sotheby's says its own "extensive research" has not established this, but that it will work with the family to try and reach a solution. "Sotheby's takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the ownership history of Châtaigniers en fleurs," the auction house told the BBC in a statement. "We are aware of the concerns recently raised by representatives of the Fischer heirs and have been in dialogue with them regarding the painting's history. "While our research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, we recognise the importance of engaging thoughtfully and constructively with the family and are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution." The painting is being sold as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection. Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890. It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934. The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotherby's says. Four other owners have had it prior to it being put up for auction this year. Fischer family heirs have instructed a lawyer who, according to the New York Times , has written to Sotherby's on their behalf. He is said to have told the auction house the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment. This article originally appeared on BBC at https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cmwy05gg75lvo?xtor=AL-72-%5Bpartner%5D-%5Byahoo.north.america%5D-%5Bheadline%5D-%5Bnews%5D-%5Bbizdev%5D-%5Bisapi%5D

item.title: El Niño could become the strongest on record, with wild weather lasting into 2027
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The surging El Niño continues to make news. The current El Niño climate pattern has reached the top of the scale for intensity, according to a report released Nov. 12 from NOAA's Climate Prediction Center (CPC) . The pattern is now considered to be "very strong" – the highest of the CPC's four El Niño intensity categories. Only three other El Niños on record have attained this level: 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16. Modern El Niño records started in 1950. Chances for a historic event exceeding those previous El Niños are now about 60%, remaining at better than even odds, the CPC said . El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon in which surface waters in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, causing weather extremes around the world, including drought in some regions and heavy rainfall in others. But how long will this El Niño last? How long will its impacts on the weather be felt? And is La Niña next? USA TODAY turned to an expert for answers. When is El Niño expected to peak? The El Niño is projected to peak later in 2026, or early in 2027, according to Michelle L'Heureux , a physical scientist with the National Weather Service's extended prediction division. "Right now, it looks like it will peak during the October-December or November-January periods or 'seasons,'" said L'Heureux, who also serves as NOAA's ENSO team lead, in an email to USA TODAY. "For our purposes, a season is any 3-month average which we monitor to evaluate the state of ENSO." ENSO stands for "El Niño-Southern Oscillation," which is the overall term for the entire El Niño/La Niña/neutral cycle. How long is this El Niño expected to last? According to L'Heureux, it's expected to continue into spring: "Our latest ENSO update favors the return of ENSO-neutral, with a 61% chance during the April-June period. There is also a 38% chance of El Nino continuing through that period." How long will El Niño continue to disrupt global weather patterns? The "very strong" El Niño event is set to unleash even more heat and extreme weather well into 2027, according to a report released last week from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) . "El Niño releases heat from the ocean and is expected to increase the risk of extreme heat, drought and heavy rainfall well into 2027," according to a WMO release . It is also expected to raise global temperatures to near-record levels. El Niño typically has the greatest impact on global average temperatures in the year after its development, the WMO said. L'Heureux agrees, noting that, "globally I would expect impacts through at least the spring. As the sea-surface temperatures cool in the tropical Pacific, we will still see lagged influences from El Niño – sometimes these effects can be quite significant even as the ocean temperatures cool." "This is because the El Niño can interact with other meteorological features like the monsoons and jet streams, which may have different timing from the sea surface temperature peak of El Niño itself," she said. Is a shift to La Niña possible after El Niño ends? "Yes, our official outlook opens the door to the development of La Niña in later 2027," L'Heureux said. "The odds of La Niña are 33% during June-August 2027, which is the longest forecast horizon NOAA officially predicts. But it is not unusual for strong El Niño events to transition into a La Niña by the following winter." La Niña is El Niño's opposite pattern, which is marked by cooler-than-average sea water in the tropical Pacific Ocean. If La Niña develops and persists into next fall, this could boost the chances for an active 2027 Atlantic hurricane season, which would be in sharp contrast to this year's moribund season. El Niño is still large and in charge Experts say that El Niño will be the dominant driver of U.S. weather for the near future: "El Niño will remain in control of the weather pattern for the next several months," DTN meteorologist John Baranick said in an online forecast report released Nov. 11. How has El Niño impacted the USA's weather so far? The fall season has been one of active weather from the Southwest to the Upper Midwest, Baranick said. "Storm systems coming off of the Pacific Ocean have generally led to a storm track that favored these areas more than the rest of the country." "This is heavily influenced by El Niño," he said. "With El Niño peaking over the next couple of months, this type of pattern is generally to be expected, though the storm track generally pushes across the southern tier of the country during the winter season." Where El Niño could have the biggest U.S. impacts this winter Southern Plains, Southeast and mid-Atlantic: An active southern storm track could bring frequent rain from the southern Plains through the Southeast and into the mid-Atlantic, AccuWeather said . "Flooding concerns could increase across the lower Mississippi and Tennessee Valleys as winter progresses, with rivers starting below normal potentially reaching flood levels by spring. Some storms could also produce severe thunderstorms and tornadoes," AccuWeather said. Western mountains: Not all El Niño impacts are bad: More snow than last winter could benefit ski resorts and help replenish rivers and reservoirs as snow melts during spring and summer. Midwest, Great Lakes and Northeast: According to AccuWeather, warmer conditions and below-average snowfall are forecast across much of the region. Fewer sustained cold outbreaks could reduce heating demand, but significant snowstorms remain possible from late January into February. California: Repeated atmospheric rivers could increase flooding and landslide risks while delivering heavy Sierra Nevada snow. Strong storms could also produce high winds and coastal flooding. In between storms, coastal flooding looks likely along the California coast due to the already elevated water levels due to the very strong El Niño. Contributing: Reuters Doyle Rice is a national correspondent for USA TODAY, with a focus on weather and climate. This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: El Niño still growing stronger. Here's what could happen next This article originally appeared on USA TODAY at https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/weather/2026/11/15/el-nino-peak-forecast/92739777007/
